cover.question: Why did he paint her dead?
cover.name: CLAUDE MONET
cover.answered_by: He couldn't stop studying the colours death put on her face (Monet's own account to Clemenceau): blue, yellow, grey

facts.claim: Monet painted his wife Camille on her deathbed: Camille sur son lit de mort, 1879, oil on canvas, Musée d'Orsay (RF 1963 3)
'Just after she died': in Monet's own account the colours were those death 'had just imposed' on her motionless face
Camille is the woman in Woman with a Parasol – Madame Monet and Her Son (1875, National Gallery of Art, Washington), with their son Jean
Their second son Michel was born on 17 March 1878 and Camille's poor health worsened; much of Monet's money went on her medical care
Camille died on 5 September 1879 in Vétheuil, aged 32 (born 15 January 1847); the cause is uncertain, so the reel doesn't name one

Monet later told his friend Georges Clemenceau that at her bedside he caught himself mechanically studying the colours death had put on her face: blue, yellow, grey (published in Clemenceau's Claude Monet: Les Nymphéas, 1928)
He described it as a reflex, in spite of himself ('couldn't stop studying')
Monet kept the painting; it stayed with his son Michel, went to the Louvre in 1963 (gift of Katia Granoff) and to the Musée d'Orsay in 1986
Supporting images: Monet's Road to Vétheuil in snow (1879) and Nadar's photograph of Monet (1899)

caption:
Monet painted his wife Camille just after she died.

Camille Doncieux had been his model since the 1860s. She is the woman in the green dress (1866) and the woman with the parasol (1875), walking on a windy hill with their son Jean. After their second son, Michel, was born in March 1878, her health got worse, and much of what Monet earned went on her care. She died in Vétheuil, on the Seine, on 5 September 1879. She was 32.

Monet sat by her bed and painted her face under the veil in quick strokes of violet, blue and white. Years later he confessed it to his friend Georges Clemenceau: at her bedside he caught himself, almost mechanically, noting the colours death had just put on her face. Blue, yellow, grey. His painter's eye wouldn't switch off, even then.

He kept the painting. It stayed in the family, came to the Louvre in 1963 and has hung in the Musée d'Orsay since 1986.
